newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel accused over Jerusalem residency policy.
newsitem.headline: Israel accused over Jerusalem residency policy.

text.p: Israeli human rights groups issued a report on Monday accusing the Jewish state of quietly trying to deport thousands of Palestinian residents of East Jerusalem in a bid to tighten its grip on all of the city.

The B'Tselem and Hamoked groups said the Interior Ministry began 18 months ago to revoke the permanent residency status of "hundreds, if not thousands" of Palestinians in East Jerusalem who had lived outside the city at one point and returned home.

"The quiet deportation is a direct continuation of Israel's overall policy in East Jerusalem since 1967 whose goal is to create a demographic and geographic reality so that Israel's sovereignty cannot be challenged," the report said.

"There are no (deportation) trucks or jeeps -- not yet -- but people are being turned into illegal aliens, hiding out in their own city," Eliahu Abrams, an attorney and Hamoked activist, told a news conference.
As designated outcasts, their Israeli-issued identity cards can be revoked, denying them access to social services.
The report said that from 1967, when Israel captured East Jerusalem, to 1994, it routinely renewed residency permits of Arab residents who travelled to live or work in other countries.
"Only a stay of seven consecutive years abroad, without visits to Israel, was liable to result in the revocation of resident status," the report said.

But 18 months ago, the Interior Ministry, relying on what the report called a broader interpretation of the law, began to revoke residency permits regardless of the time spent living outside of the city.

"All Palestinians who have lived outside of Jerusalem for a period of time, whether in a foreign country, in another part of the West Bank, or in Jerusalem's suburbs just metres outside the municipal borders are liable to lose their rights as Jerusalem residents," the report said.

"The details of this policy remain unknown and it is unclear how much time a Palestinian must spend abroad before the Interior Ministry informs the person that he or she is no longer a resident of Jerusalem," it said.
Most of East Jerusalem's 160,000 residents are permanent, having rejected the option of becoming Israeli citizens.

Jewish settlement in the Arab part of the city is at the centre of the current crisis between Israel and the PLO. Israel regards all of Jerusalem as its capital. The PLO wants East Jerusalem as capital of a Palestinian state.
An Interior Ministry response attached to the report said Israel was not involved in a forced transfer.
"Permanent residency is a matter of the reality of life and, as the Supreme Court held, when this reality no longer exists, the permit provided pursuant to that status expires," it said.

"When permanent residents sever their connection with Israel -- maintain their centre of life in another location, where they work, maintain their family life -- their free choice causes the expiration of their permanent residency," the statement said.
Such rules do not affect most of the Jews who immigrate to Israel. Under the Law of Return, they are automatically granted Israeli citizenship.
